raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic systolic heart failure syndrome presenting toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, in the absence of another identifiable cause. Although early descriptions emphasized onset within 1 month before and 5 months after delivery [1], contemporary definitions focus on new left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction, typically LV ejection fraction (LVEF) <45%, occurring in temporal relation to pregnancy [2-6]. PPCM is clinically important because it affects young women, may present abruptly with pulmonary edema, arrhythmia, thromboembolism, cardiogenic shock, or death, yet also has a higher chance of reverse remodeling than most dilated cardiomyopathies.

Incidence varies widely by geography and ascertainment. Population-based North American studies estimate roughly 1 case per 1000–4000 live births, with increasing recognition over time [7-11]. Risk is consistently higher among women of African ancestry, and associations include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestation, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and pre-eclampsia [8-12]. These associations suggest that PPCM is not a single disease but a final common phenotype arising from vascular, inflammatory, hormonal, and genetic susceptibility.

Pathobiology has shifted from nonspecific myocarditis models toward a vascular–hormonal paradigm. In a seminal experimental study, oxidative stress and reduced cardiomyocyte STAT3 signaling promoted cathepsin D cleavage of prolactin into a 16-kDa fragment with antiangiogenic and proapoptotic effects [14]. Complementary work showed that late gestation imposes a major angiogenic stress: increased soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 and impaired proangiogenic reserve can precipitate PPCM, particularly in susceptible myocardium [15]. MicroRNA-146a has been implicated downstream of the 16-kDa prolactin fragment and may serve as both mediator and biomarker [16]. In parallel, familial clustering and sequencing studies demonstrate overlap with dilated cardiomyopathy, especially truncating variants in TTN and other cardiomyopathy genes [17-20]. Thus, PPCM can be conceptualized as pregnancy-triggered cardiomyopathy in which peripartum vascular stress unmasks acquired or inherited myocardial vulnerability.

Diagnosis requires suspicion because dyspnea, edema, and fatigue overlap with normal pregnancy. Red flags include orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, tachycardia out of proportion, hypoxemia, elevated jugular venous pressure, new murmur, S3, pulmonary edema, or embolic events. Echocardiography is central, documenting LVEF, LV size, right ventricular function, valvular regurgitation, pulmonary pressures, and thrombus. Natriuretic peptides are useful because marked elevation is not expected in uncomplicated pregnancy. Cardiac magnetic resonance can help when myocarditis, infarction, infiltrative disease, or thrombus is uncertain, although gadolinium is generally avoided during pregnancy. Differential diagnoses include pre-existing dilated cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, congenital heart disease, pulmonary embolism, acute coronary syndrome including spontaneous coronary artery dissection, sepsis-related cardiomyopathy, and hypertensive pulmonary edema.

Prognosis is heterogeneous. In the North American IPAC cohort, recovery was common but strongly related to baseline LVEF and LV size; women presenting with LVEF <30% or marked LV dilation had lower likelihood of full recovery [21]. South African, German, and other cohorts similarly identify lower initial LVEF, larger LV dimensions, right ventricular dysfunction, delayed diagnosis, and non-recovery by 6 months as adverse markers [22-24]. Contemporary care has improved survival, but severe presentations still require intensive monitoring, inotropes, temporary mechanical circulatory support, durable LV assist devices, or transplantation [25].

Treatment follows guideline-directed heart failure therapy adapted for pregnancy and lactation. During pregnancy, beta-blockers, hydralazine–nitrate combinations, loop diuretics, digoxin, and anticoagulation when indicated are commonly used, while angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are avoided until after delivery. Postpartum, standard heart failure therapy should be rapidly optimized, considering breastfeeding compatibility and shared decision-making. Anticoagulation is generally considered when LVEF is severely reduced, LV thrombus is present, atrial fibrillation occurs, or bromocriptine is used, because pregnancy, puerperium, and severe LV dysfunction are prothrombotic.

Bromocriptine, a dopamine agonist that suppresses prolactin secretion, is biologically plausible and supported by a pilot randomized study in severe PPCM [26] and a subsequent multicenter randomized trial comparing shorter and longer regimens [27]. Its use remains variable internationally: it may be considered in moderate-to-severe PPCM, especially early postpartum, but should be accompanied by anticoagulation and counseling about lactation suppression. Registry data underscore global heterogeneity in presentation, treatment, and outcomes, with many women outside high-resource settings receiving delayed diagnosis or incomplete heart failure therapy [28,29].

Future pregnancy counseling is essential. Subsequent pregnancy carries relapse risk, particularly if LV function has not normalized. Even after apparent recovery, recurrent LV dysfunction can occur; therefore, preconception evaluation, avoidance of pregnancy when LVEF remains reduced, and close cardio-obstetric surveillance are recommended [30]. Long-term follow-up is warranted because “recovered” PPCM may represent remission rather than cure, especially in women with genetic predisposition or residual LV dilation. Multidisciplinary care, equitable access to echocardiography and heart failure medicines, and research integrating genomics, vascular biology, and global registries are central to improving maternal outcomes.
